## Alaska Psychiatric Institute, Anchorage. Patient: Ian Demme, 18 y.o.

Initial Psychological Evaluation

Patient exhibits severe psychological trauma consistent with acute emotional distress following the recent termination of a long-term romantic relationship. Clinical presentation includes profound depression, emotional withdrawal, survivor's guilt related to the disappearance of five local children, insomnia, and persistent anxiety.

Following the disappearance of the five children in August 2008, Ian Demme was discovered unconscious deep in the woods surrounding Mag Point with a large shard of glass in his left forearm. He had suffered severe blood loss and barely survived. Investigators concluded that the wound had been self-inflicted and ruled the incident a failed suicide attempt brought on by severe psychological trauma (his girlfriend left him abruptly, leaving Mag Point for good). With no evidence to suggest otherwise, Ian was committed to the *Alaska Psychiatric Institute* for psychiatric evaluation and treatment. In reality, Ian had never intended to take his own life. The reason behind his actions was an attempt to save abducted child. During his stay at the institution, he encountered another patient, August Pruett, a former military officer. ## The town > "The first thing you'll notice about Mag Point is the fog. The last thing you'll remember is what you saw inside it." {/* ============ 1 · ATMOSPHERE ============ */} Mag Point is a remote coastal town on Baranof Island in Southeast Alaska, a place where civilization ends and the wilderness begins. Wedged between towering mountain ridges and the icy waters of the Gulf of Alaska, it spends much of the year beneath heavy clouds, relentless rain, and endless winter nights. Sunshine is a rare luxury reserved for the brief summer months. Thick coastal fog drifts in from the sea throughout the year, but in August it becomes almost unnatural, blanketing the town and surrounding forests for days at a time. Once a thriving fishing and oil town, Mag Point has spent decades in slow decline. Young people leave in search of a better future, businesses struggle to survive, and abandoned buildings stand as reminders of more prosperous days. The town has earned a grim reputation among outsiders. Since the late 1980s, Mag Point has been plagued by a series of unexplained disappearances. Many dismiss them as unfortunate accidents caused by the unforgiving Alaskan wilderness or attribute them to the nearby Alaska Triangle, a region infamous for mysterious vanishings and unsolved cases. The greatest tragedy came in August 2008, when five young children vanished within days of one another, shattering the community. A decade later, in 2018, the disappearances begin again, drawing investigators into a mystery that reaches far beyond missing persons. In this story, Mag Point is more than a setting. It is a character in its own right: a lonely, weather-beaten town where every August the fog returns, bringing with it questions no one has ever been able to answer. {/* ============ 2 · HISTORY (collapsible) ============ */}

The Russian Frontier (1805–1867)

Mag Point was founded in 1805 by Russian explorer Vasiliy Sokolov. Originally known as Fort Mag Point, it served as the easternmost military and trading outpost of the Russian-American Company on Baranof Island. The settlement occupied a narrow strip of land between steep mountain ridges and the sea, making it both naturally protected and strategically important. Ships departing from its harbor carried explorers, hunters, missionaries, and supplies deeper into the Alaskan frontier. The fort remained small but prosperous, becoming known for its skilled shipwrights, fisheries, and timber trade.


Under American Rule (1867–1897)

Following the United States' purchase of Alaska in 1867, Mag Point peacefully transitioned to American administration. Many Russian settlers remained, leaving behind an architectural and cultural legacy still visible throughout the town. The harbor continued to grow as a regional shipping stop, while fishing gradually replaced the fur trade as the town's primary industry.


The Gold Rush Boom (1897–1915)

Although no major gold deposits were discovered near Mag Point itself, the town became an important supply port during the Klondike Gold Rush. Hotels, warehouses, saloons, banks, and shipping companies appeared almost overnight as thousands of prospectors passed through on their way north. At its peak, Mag Point was one of southeastern Alaska's busiest coastal settlements. When the Gold Rush ended, many newcomers stayed, helping transform the temporary frontier town into a permanent community.


A Fishing Town (1915–1929)

With mining in decline, Mag Point embraced commercial fishing. Large canneries, shipyards, and seafood processing facilities were built along the waterfront, while schools, churches, parks, and civic buildings reshaped the growing town. The original Russian fort was dismantled during this period, with only a monument to its founder, Vasiliy Sokolov, remaining in the town square.


Decline and Recovery (1929–1970)

The Great Depression severely affected Mag Point. Businesses closed, unemployment soared, and many families left in search of work elsewhere. The town slowly recovered after World War II as military contracts, improved infrastructure, and renewed fishing activity brought jobs back to the region. New roads, neighborhoods, and public buildings modernized much of the aging settlement.


Oil and Prosperity (1970–1990)

The discovery of offshore oil led to another economic boom. "Shoreside Petroleum" established operations near Mag Point, creating hundreds of jobs alongside the already thriving fishing industry. By the early 1980s, the population had reached nearly 25,000, making Mag Point one of the largest towns in southeastern Alaska. Modern schools, a hospital, expanded harbor facilities, and private businesses reflected the town's newfound prosperity. Yet during the late 1970s, a handful of unusual events began to circulate among locals. Hunters occasionally reported strange lights deep in the mountains. Fishermen described hearing distant voices over calm waters where no boats were present. Unexplained radio interference was dismissed as a natural anomaly, becoming little more than local folklore.


Modern Times (1990–now)

By the early 1990s, Mag Point entered a long period of economic decline. Fish stocks became less reliable, oil production slowed, and many of the town's largest employers began reducing their workforce. Younger generations left for larger Alaskan cities or the mainland in search of better opportunities.

By 2008, the population had fallen from nearly 25,000 to approximately 15,000, leaving Mag Point struggling to preserve its identity. Around the same time, unsettling rumors began to spread. A handful of unexplained disappearances that had started in the late Cold War years became more frequent, though never numerous enough to attract national attention. Local authorities investigated each case individually, attributing them to accidents, harsh wilderness conditions, or people leaving town without notice. Among residents, however, whispers persisted that something darker had taken root in Mag Point.

Despite its decline, the town remains alive. Its harbor still served a modest fishing fleet, "Shoreside Petroleum" maintained regional operations, and family-owned businesses fought to survive alongside aging hotels, restaurants, and seafood processing facilities. To outsiders, Mag Point was simply another struggling Alaskan coastal town.

To its residents, it was a place that had never quite let go of its past.
